source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3):435-502 (target article plus open peer commentary)
finding: Thagard states seven principles of explanatory coherence: symmetry, explanation, analogy, data priority, contradiction, acceptability, system coherence. Coherence is first a pairwise relation between two propositions. Explanation is the main source of links. The more hypotheses it takes to explain something, the weaker each link.
numbers: Principle 2(c): degree of coherence is inversely proportional to the number of propositions doing the explaining. Seven principles in section 2.2.
limits: Explanation is taken as a primitive. The theory gives no account of how hypotheses are formed, only how they are chosen among.
agent_relevance: This is the spec for a code-run selector: scoring candidate rules by what they explain, penalised by how many extra assumptions they need. It gives a concrete, checkable form to coverage plus simplicity.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3):435-502 (target article plus open peer commentary)
finding: ECHO turns the principles into a network. Each proposition is a unit. Coherence becomes a symmetric excitatory link, incoherence a symmetric inhibitory link. A special evidence unit stuck at activation 1 feeds the data units (data priority). Units settle and positive activation means accept, negative means reject.
numbers: Default parameters in all reported runs: excitation .05, inhibition -.2 (tolerance .25), data excitation .1, decay .05, simplicity impact 1, analogy impact 1. Activation range -1 to 1. Most networks settle in under 100 cycles; Copernicus vs Ptolemy (over 150 units) needed about 210 cycles.
quote: Typically, ECHO is run with excitatory weights set at .05
limits: Parameters are set by the programmer. Thagard says they could be learned but did not do it.
agent_relevance: The whole selector is a few lines of code: build links from (explain, contradict, data) triples, iterate, read the sign. The LLM would only emit the triples. Code does the choosing (G5).

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3):435-502 (target article plus open peer commentary)
finding: Sensitivity analysis: behaviour holds over a wide range of parameters. Real limits exist. If excitation is too high relative to inhibition, ECHO stops rejecting inferior hypotheses (too much tolerance). If excitation is far higher it oscillates and fails to settle.
numbers: Table 11 (as extracted; the row order in the text layer is scrambled): Lavoisier network settled in 107 cycles, Darwin in 49. Lavoisier: no important change when decay, excitation, inhibition and data excitation were each halved or doubled. Oscillation seen in the Chambers case when excitation = .17 instead of .05.
limits: Sensitivity was run by the author on four of his own cases. No independent robustness test.
agent_relevance: A selector of this type has a known failure: if support is too strong relative to conflict, rival rules all survive. Our code should log whether the rival was actually driven below zero, not only which unit is highest.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3):435-502 (target article plus open peer commentary)
finding: Legal application 1, Chambers (Central Park 'preppy' murder, 1988). Input came from New York Times daily reports. ECHO gave a clear win to the hypothesis that Chambers strangled the victim. The real jury never finished: a manslaughter plea was agreed during deliberation. Thagard notes ECHO does not model 'beyond a reasonable doubt'.
numbers: Hypotheses: G1-G7 (guilt) vs I1-I8 (innocence); evidence E0-E16. Reasonable doubt would need extra activation on innocence hypotheses or a high tolerance level.
limits: No verdict exists to compare with. The match is to a plausible outcome only, and the input was coded by the author from press accounts.
agent_relevance: Shows the gap between 'best explanation wins' and a burden-of-proof rule. A code selector needs a separate threshold (accept only if the winner beats the rival by a margin), which we can set per task.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3):435-502 (target article plus open peer commentary)
finding: Legal application 2, Peyer (Cara Knott murder, San Diego, 1988). The real jury hung: seven for second-degree murder, five against. ECHO found more coherence in the guilt hypotheses, but did not strongly reject the innocence hypothesis. Thagard offers burden of proof and extraneous factors (a juror said a 13-year patrolman could never murder) as reasons for the split.
numbers: Jury split 7 to 5. Sensitivity analyses (Table 11 in Appendix) show ECHO rejects innocence much less strongly for Peyer than for Chambers.
limits: Post-hoc reading of a mixed result. A hung jury is weak evidence for a model: it fits any weak margin.
agent_relevance: A small win margin should be reported as 'unresolved', not as a verdict. Useful rule for S7-style choice: if the winner's margin is small, do not select; gather another check.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3):435-502 (target article plus open peer commentary)
finding: Author admits the main limit: all propositions, explain links and contradiction links are typed in by the programmer. Several people did ECHO analyses on over a dozen cases, with 'virtually no adjustment' of input in the four main examples. No test of intercoder reliability was done.
numbers: 'More than a dozen' disparate cases; four detailed examples (Lavoisier, Darwin, Chambers, Peyer). Intercoder reliability: not tested.
quote: We have not yet done the experiment of having several people analyze the same case
limits: Encoding freedom is the main way a coherence model can be made to fit anything. The Detail Maxim is the only guard: analyse all rivals at the same level of detail.
agent_relevance: In our agent the LLM does the encoding, so encoding noise is the risk. Use the Detail Maxim as a code check: require the same number of explain edges per rival before running the network.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3):435-502 (target article plus open peer commentary)
finding: Psychological testability was only proposed, not shown. Thagard cites Ranney and Thagard (1988), where ECHO was run on verbal protocols of students learning projectile physics and captured belief revisions, and plans studies where subjects' confidence is compared with ECHO activations. He ties ECHO to attribution theory, discourse processing and conceptual change.
numbers: No subject-level numbers given in this paper for ECHO vs human confidence in 1989.
limits: As of 1989 the claim was 'suggestive', in the author's words, not tested with controlled experiments.
agent_relevance: Do not claim a coherence selector is human-like. Treat it as a design choice and measure it on our own logs.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3):435-502 (target article plus open peer commentary)
finding: Open peer commentary raised sharp objections. Achinstein: the theory is empty if 'explain' stays undefined, and rival theories can fit the same data. A psychologist commentator: 'explains' could be replaced by 'connected to' and nothing in the model would change. McDermott: the work is energy minimisation, not connectionism. Dawes: Bayesian models are order-free while the Pennington-Hastie story model predicts order effects, and Thagard should keep his basic binary hypothesis.
numbers: Commentaries by Achinstein, Dawes, McDermott and others in the same issue (pp. 464 onward).
limits: Thagard replied to these in the issue; replies not read this session.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'explains' is the weak point. For code we need a checkable definition (for example: rule predicts the observed output on this example), not a model's feeling that it explains.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3):435-502 (target article plus open peer commentary)
finding: Chi's commentary argues that ECHO's account of belief change in Ranney's physics data hides the hard step. Child and student learning work suggests that confronting someone with contradicting evidence does not usually make them drop the hypothesis. The key step is realising that a hypothesis explains a given piece of evidence, and ECHO takes that as given.
numbers: Qualitative argument; Chi cites Piagetian research on rejection of hypotheses.
limits: Commentary, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: a revision must be triggered by real output. A network will flip when edges change, so the risk is in who writes the edges.

source: Thagard and Verbeurgt (1998) Coherence as constraint satisfaction. Cognitive Science 22(1):1-24
finding: Defines coherence as splitting elements into accepted and rejected sets so that the most constraint weight is satisfied. Positive constraint: both accepted or both rejected. Negative constraint: exactly one accepted. Proves the problem is NP-hard by reduction from MAX CUT. Lists five algorithms: exhaustive, incremental, connectionist, greedy, semidefinite programming.
numbers: SDP algorithm gives expected satisfied weight at least 0.878 of optimal (0.87856, Goemans-Williamson). The older incremental method guarantees only 0.5. Connectionist method has no guarantee. Authors report 'a dozen coherence problems' in Table 1.
limits: Authors tested SDP and greedy against the connectionist method only on their own examples. Results match except in ties.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean formal object for code selection: maximise satisfied constraint weight. For our small graphs (tens of nodes) exhaustive search over accept/reject is feasible and exact, so no connectionist run is needed.

source: Thagard and Verbeurgt (1998) Coherence as constraint satisfaction. Cognitive Science 22(1):1-24
finding: Greedy algorithm: start from random accept/reject, flip whichever element most increases satisfied weight, repeat until no flip helps. On the authors' tested examples it gives the same accepted set as the connectionist ECHO, except that ties are broken randomly. Authors note connectionist update can fail to converge in general and cite results for Hopfield and Boltzmann networks.
numbers: Convergence results cited: asynchronous Hopfield updates converge to a local optimum with symmetric weights (Hopfield 1982); synchronous ECHO-style updates have no general guarantee.
limits: Greedy and local search can stick in local optima. Only tested on the authors' own cases.
agent_relevance: A flip-based local search with random restarts is simpler and more reliable than iterative activation. Run it several times and report whether all runs agree (agreement across restarts is a real check, unlike agreement across LLM samples, G4).

source: Thagard (2004) Causal inference in legal decision making: explanatory coherence vs. Bayesian networks. Applied Artificial Intelligence 18:231-249
finding: Models both von Bulow trials with ECHO. Trial 1 (1982, convicted of assault with intent to murder) and trial 2 (1985, acquitted). ECHO accepts 'Claus injected Sunny with insulin' for trial 1 and rejects it for trial 2. In trial 2 the change in input was undermined witness testimony, expert evidence against insulin as cause, and a weaker motive. Both the connectionist and greedy algorithms agree.
numbers: Trial 1 network: 188 update cycles to settle; greedy needed about 16 flips. Parameters in this paper: excitation .04, inhibition -.06. A student's simulation of the 1684 Braddon trial had over 200 propositions and settled in a few minutes on a laptop.
limits: Both outcomes are known and the author built the input, with knowledge of the outcomes. This is retrodiction, not prediction. Only two verdicts.
agent_relevance: Shows ECHO flips when testimony is undermined by giving witnesses alternative explanations. For us: an observation can be defused by adding a competing explanation of why it was reported, and code can recompute the choice.

source: Thagard (2004) Causal inference in legal decision making: explanatory coherence vs. Bayesian networks. Applied Artificial Intelligence 18:231-249
finding: Head-to-head with a Bayesian network (JavaBayes) on trial 1. Thagard guessed conditional probabilities: .7 for 'witness says X given X is true', and left unknown cells at the default .5. The network still gave P(Claus injected) above .5 and P(Sunny self-injected) below .5, matching the guilty verdict. He argues the Bayesian route has an interpretation problem (what do the numbers mean) and an implementation problem (2^(n-1) conditional probabilities per node with n parents).
numbers: Example: node C-injected with three parents needed eight conditional probabilities, most set to .5 by default. No Bayesian run was made for trial 2.
limits: The Bayes arm is weak: probabilities were guessed by the author, not elicited or fitted. The comparison shows effort, not accuracy. Both approaches reproduce trial 1.
agent_relevance: Fair warning for us: a coherence network and a Bayes net can agree. The coherence version needs no numbers, which suits an LLM that cannot give calibrated probabilities. But neither is validated against ground truth here.

source: Thagard (2003) Why wasn't O.J. convicted? Emotional coherence in legal inference. Cognition and Emotion 17(3):361-383
finding: A failure of pure explanatory coherence. Given the Simpson trial evidence, ECHO accepts that Simpson was the killer, and also accepts that the LAPD tried to frame him. The real jury acquitted. A JavaBayes network also said guilty. Thagard then adds hot cognition (HOTCO 2): small valence links, positive to 'O.J. is good' and negative to 'LAPD is good', flip the output to acquittal.
numbers: ECHO: guilty and framed accepted. JavaBayes: P(OJ killed Nicole | evidence) = .72, P(drug killings) = .29, P(LAPD framed) = .99, from about 60 hand-set conditional probabilities. HOTCO 2: default .05 valence link flips ECHO to reject guilt. Presumption of innocence in ECHO: guilt unit rejected if inhibition exceeds .065, against the .05 data excitation.
limits: Single case. Valence values were tuned by the author after seeing the verdict. Thagard says deleting the defence's frame-up explanations makes HOTCO find Simpson guilty, so evidence still matters.
agent_relevance: A coherence network is also a bias amplifier: a small prior on a few nodes can flip the winner. In our agent a prior (such as the model's liking for a rule) must not enter the network. Keep the node set free of preference links.

source: Thagard (2005) Testimony, credibility, and explanatory coherence. Erkenntnis 63:295-316
finding: Proposes a two-path account of testimony. Default path: accept the claim automatically if it is consistent with beliefs and the source seems credible. Reflective path: if not, judge it by explanatory coherence, treating 'the speaker believes it because it is true' against 'mistaken or lying'. Shown by simulation on real-life cases and argued as better than a Bayesian account.
numbers: Simulations on a business-forum case; no participant data in this paper.
limits: Descriptive claims about default acceptance cite other work, not new experiments here.
agent_relevance: The two-path form matches G1: do the cheap thing by default, run the heavier coherence check only on a signal such as a conflict or an untrusted source.

source: Thagard (2006) Evaluating explanations in law, science, and everyday life. Current Directions in Psychological Science 15(3)
finding: A short review. It says ECHO has been applied to many legal, scientific and everyday cases, and lists the support: Read and Marcus-Newhall (1993) found social explanations follow explanatory coherence principles; Simon (2004) reviews legal decision experiments readily read as coherence; Ranney and Schank (1998) on student science reasoning; Kunda and Thagard (1996) on stereotypes with a similar network.
numbers: No new numbers. Describes HOTCO reproducing the Simpson acquittal.
limits: Self-review by the model's author. The listed human studies were not opened here (see lines on Simon).
agent_relevance: Index of where to look for human tests of the model. Primary human data is in Read and Marcus-Newhall (1993) and Simon and colleagues, not in Thagard's own simulations.

source: Thagard (1992) Adversarial problem solving: modeling an opponent using explanatory coherence. Cognitive Science 16:123-149
finding: Applies ECHO to inferring an opponent's plans, with deception as the hard case. Simulates the USS Vincennes decision (1988) to fire on an aircraft that proved to be an Iranian airliner. ECHO rejects the airliner hypothesis and accepts the F-14 attack hypothesis, as the captain did.
numbers: Vincennes network stabilised after 60 update cycles. The F-14 hypothesis explained seven pieces of evidence, the airliner hypothesis two; the higher-level hypothesis that Iran planned an attack also feeds activation.
limits: Input built from the official report. Another retrodiction. Thagard notes breadth alone does not explain the result; a hypothesis being explained by a higher hypothesis also matters.
agent_relevance: Illustrates a hazard: a network confidently selects a wrong hypothesis when the evidence list is wrong (the descending-aircraft report was false). Garbage in the data nodes gives a confident error, so verify data nodes by code (G3).

source: Thagard (2007) Coherence, truth, and the development of scientific knowledge. Philosophy of Science
finding: Argues coherence of the explanatory kind (mechanisms) leads to approximate truth. Rejects the route through probability: Olsson and Shogenji analyses of coherence in probability terms, he says, fail on interpretation, realisation and implementation.
numbers: No experiment. Cites his 2004 comparison for the implementation problem.
limits: Philosophical argument. Probabilistic coherence researchers (Olsson, Bovens and Hartmann) hold that coherence need not raise truth probability; this document does not engage their formal results beyond a dismissal.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a high coherence score as a probability of being right. Coherent wrong stories exist (see O.J. and Vincennes lines).

source: Holyoak and Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction. J Exp Psychol: General 128(1):3-31
finding: Founding human experiments on coherence shifts in legal-style cases. Known from citations: people read a legal case, and as they lean to one verdict they re-rate the evidence to fit it (bidirectional reasoning). Modelled with a constraint-satisfaction network. Crossref gives no abstract and the paper was not reachable; this line is a lead only.
numbers: Not read. No numbers recorded.
limits: Paywalled (APA); the PDF link returned 403. Do not quote numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Core human study to read next for the 'coherence shift' effect size before relying on it.

source: Simon, Krawczyk and Holyoak (2004) Construction of preferences by constraint satisfaction. Psychological Science 15(5)
finding: Abstract only (Crossref). Participants chose between two multi-attribute job offers. Attribute preferences were measured before, during and after the choice. Preferences shifted to cohere with the eventual choice: chosen option's attributes rated higher, rejected option's lower. The shift came before commitment. A single decisive attribute triggered it in Experiment 1; in Experiment 2 it arose with no decisive attribute.
numbers: Two experiments (job-offer choice). Sample sizes and effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only; full text paywalled (SAGE returned 403). Semantic Scholar lists 226 citations.
agent_relevance: Key worry for us: the same shift may occur inside an LLM chain of thought. Once a favoured rule emerges, the model may rate its own evidence as stronger. Counter: freeze evidence scores in code before the option is chosen.

source: Glockner (2010 online) Coherence shifts in probabilistic inference tasks. J Behavioral Decision Making
finding: Abstract only (Crossref). Tests the parallel constraint satisfaction (PCS) model against fast-and-frugal heuristics. PCS predicts cue validities change during judgment to support the favoured option; heuristics predict they stay fixed. Coherence shifts were found with weather forecast cues and city-size tasks. Cue validity measured before, after (Exp. 1) and during judgment (Exp. 2 and 3).
numbers: Three experiments. Sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Written by a PCS proponent; heuristic-model defenders may disagree.
agent_relevance: Confirms coherence shifts outside law. Supports the design rule: fix evidence weights before comparing rivals.

source: Glockner and colleagues (2016) Information search, coherence shifts and their interplay for legal decision making (SSRN 2816609)
finding: Abstract only (Crossref). Four studies, three legal cases each, with free information search. Strong coherence shifts in every study. Against expectation, people mostly searched for information contrary to their current belief (disconfirmatory search). Authors call the striving for coherence unconscious and hard to correct.
numbers: Four studies; sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only, an SSRN working paper. The disconfirmatory-search result partly cuts against the usual confirmation-bias story.
agent_relevance: Coherence shifts happen even when search is balanced, so 'show the model both sides' is not enough. Needs code-side freezing of evidence ratings.

source: Forst and Glockner (2026) Intuitive and deliberate decisions can be accounted for by the same cognitive process model. Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 33(2):83
finding: Preregistered online experiment, N = 128 after exclusions (67 intuition, 61 deliberation). Probabilistic inference task. The deliberation instruction lengthened decisions but did not change which strategy people used. PCS (coherence-based, parallel) fit best for the majority in both conditions.
numbers: Decision time: deliberate M = 9241 ms vs intuitive M = 5583 ms, d = 0.85. Strategy classification: 50-60% PCS, under 30% weighted additive, under 15% simple heuristics (take-the-best, equal weights). Deliberation improved adherence to the rational standard.
limits: Probabilistic inference with given cues, not legal verdicts. Authors are PCS proponents. Online sample.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to 'think harder' may speed or slow it without changing the process. Matches G1: forced extra deliberation is not a lever; a code-run check is.

source: Glockner and Jekel (2026) Cognitive reflection enhances rationality without changing the underlying cognitive processes. Behavioral Sciences 16(6):858
finding: N = 249. Each person did 250 probabilistic inference tasks and 16 risky-choice tasks. Higher Cognitive Reflection Test scores meant more rational choices. The same PCS model best explained both low and high reflection groups; high-reflection people appeared to use coherence processes more efficiently and consistently.
numbers: N = 249; 250 inference tasks and 16 risky-decision tasks per participant. Specific effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Correlational across individuals. Task design avoids trap problems, so it says nothing about CRT-type lures.
agent_relevance: Better reasoners may use the same coherence mechanism with less noise. This favours cleaning up the inputs and the arithmetic (code) rather than changing the mechanism.

source: Simon and Read (2025) Toward a general framework of biased reasoning: coherence-based reasoning. Perspectives on Psychological Science (SSRN 6561678)
finding: Abstract only (Crossref). Proposes coherence-based reasoning, run as constraint satisfaction in connectionist networks, as one framework behind confirmation bias, halo effect, stereotype spillover, hindsight bias, motivated reasoning, emotion-driven and ideological reasoning. Says the process is adaptive, and turns biased when network nodes or links are wrong, overweighted or nonnormative.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. A unifying review by the proponents; breadth of claim is also a risk of unfalsifiability.
agent_relevance: The bias is in the inputs and weights, not in the settling step. Matches our plan: audit the nodes and links in code, trust the settling.

source: Mock-juror emotion and evidence evaluation (2025). Behavioral Sciences 15(7):965 'Jurymen seldom rule against a person that they like'
finding: Three studies (N = 713, 677, 651) with mock jurors in a civil case. More negative moral emotion toward the defendant predicted agreeing more with unrelated plaintiff evidence and less with unrelated defence evidence, and then liable votes and higher damages. Judicial rehabilitation did not reduce the effect. Read as a coherence-based reasoning result.
numbers: N = 713, N = 677, N = 651 across the three studies. Emotion to evidence evaluation to verdict path.
limits: Correlational mediation in mock civil cases; self-reported emotion; the instruction (judicial rehabilitation) failed.
agent_relevance: Telling a reasoner to ignore a bias did not work. Supports removing the bias path structurally (hide author, source and preference from the scorer) rather than by instruction (G5).

source: Dalal, Valentino, Freitas, Buitelaar (2024) Inference to the best explanation in large language models. ACL 2024
finding: IBE-Eval scores competing LLM-written causal explanations with code-computed features: logical consistency (Prolog proof), parsimony (proof depth, concept drift), coherence (average NLI entailment of each If-Then step) and linguistic uncertainty (hedging). It picks the more plausible explanation better than GPT-3.5 used as a judge.
numbers: Up to 77% accuracy, 27 points above random and 17 points above the GPT-3.5-as-judge baseline (average gain 17.5 points). COPA (500 items) and a 500-item E-CARE sample; GPT-3.5, LLaMA 2 13B and 7B. Spearman with human judgment: IBE-Eval 0.64 (p<0.01), GPT-3.5 judge 0.31 (not significant). Two human evaluators picked the correct explanation 96% (COPA) and 91% (E-CARE); Cohen's kappa .68.
limits: Two-option commonsense causal questions, old models. Logical consistency was a weak signal because LLMs over-rationalise and build consistent explanations for wrong options. This 'coherence' is entailment between steps, not a Thagard network. The best score came from stacking features, which was tuned on the same data.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM test of code-scored explanation quality. Direct support for 'code selects': parsimony and step coherence predicted correctness; self-judging did worse. Warns that consistency alone is useless since the model rationalises anything.

source: Lehr, Saichandran, Harmon-Jones, Vitali, Banaji (2025) Kernels of selfhood: GPT-4o shows humanlike patterns of cognitive dissonance moderated by free choice. PNAS
finding: A coherence shift in an LLM. After GPT-4o wrote a pro-Putin or anti-Putin essay, its rating of Putin moved sharply toward the essay. The shift was bigger when the prompt gave an illusion of free choice of which essay to write, a signature of human dissonance.
numbers: Study 1 n = 150 (50 pro, 50 anti, 50 control essays). Study 2 preregistered n = 900 (150 per condition). Pro-Putin vs control d = 2.164; anti-Putin vs control d = 1.795; pro vs anti d = 3.775. Choice vs no choice: pro-Putin d = 0.981, anti-Putin d = 0.252 (P = 0.0298). Pro vs anti gap d = 4.179 with choice vs 3.229 without.
limits: One model, one topic, GPT-4o. Effects are far larger than in human dissonance work, which the authors take as irrational. The authors say it mimics dissonance and do not claim sentience. Alternative: ordinary context-window effects.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: an LLM updates its own stated evaluations to match what it just wrote, by huge margins. In any step where the model writes for a hypothesis and then scores evidence, expect inflated scores for that hypothesis. Score in a fresh context with no authorship (G5).

source: Lehr, Saichandran, Harmon-Jones, Vitali, Banaji (2025) Reply to Cummins et al. PNAS 122(35):e2518613122
finding: Cummins et al. argue the effect is a context-window effect, and say GPT-4o also shifts after merely reading an essay. The authors agree context windows matter, and run a new three-condition reading study. They say the choice versus no-choice difference is what the context-window account does not explain.
numbers: New study: 900 responses from chatgpt-4o-latest; 100 essays (50 pro, 50 anti) reused; each shown three times per condition; conditions choice-granted, no-choice, choice-disregarded; ratings on four items (leadership, impact on Russia, economic effectiveness, vision). Their prior point: a 600-word essay moved a model with millions of Putin words in training.
limits: Result numbers of the new study not extracted. This is a dispute between two groups; the Cummins et al. paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: The contested reading (it is just context) is enough for us: either way the model's own earlier text biases its later scores. That is the practical point.

source: Abduction In Silico: Large Language Models Replicate Human Inference to the Best Explanation (2026). Minds and Machines
finding: Abstract only (page was behind a paywall). Replicates Douven and Mirabile (2018) human abduction patterns with 16 models from 7 developers: sensitivity to explanation quality, suppression by alternative explanations, and the link between quality difference and confidence. New materials were built to reduce contamination. Models replicate the human patterns on both sets. Against individual humans, quality sensitivity falls inside human range.
numbers: Three experiments; 16 models; 7 developers; old and new materials. Effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Reproducing human patterns says models rank explanations like people, not that they rank them correctly.
agent_relevance: Models share the human tendency to favour better explanations and to be moved by alternatives, which is the input a coherence selector needs. Still needs a check against ground truth.

source: Benchmarking graph construction by large language models for coherence-driven inference (2025). IEEE ICDMW
finding: Lead only. By its title, it benchmarks how well LLMs build the proposition graphs (positive and negative constraints) that a coherence-driven inference solver needs. No abstract was retrievable (Crossref empty, IEEE page empty to the fetcher).
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Title only. Not opened.
agent_relevance: This is the exact bottleneck for our use: can the LLM write a faithful explain/contradict graph. Open the paper next before building.
